**Video:** [Lec 44 — Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) as Regularized MLP](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mSYTyrXCsA8)

## Learning goals

- View a **CNN** as a multilayer net whose layers are convolutions (local + shared weights), nonlinearities, and often pooling.
- Interpret convolution / pooling as **architectural regularization** of a fully connected MLP.
- Sketch forward computation: feature maps $\to$ activation $\to$ downsample $\to$ repeat $\to$ dense head.
- Connect back to ERM: same backprop story, structured $\theta$.

## Before this clicks

Lecture 43 introduced local receptive fields and parameter sharing. A CNN makes those ideas the default layer type. Compared with a dense MLP on flattened images, many MLP weights are forced to zero (no long-range connections in early layers) and many remaining weights are **tied** (same filter everywhere). That is regularization by construction: we optimize over a smaller, vision-shaped subset of all possible nets.

---

## Main ideas

### 1. Convolutional layer

Input feature map(s) $h$, kernel bank $K$. Output channel $c$ at location $(i,j)$:

$$
z^{(c)}_{i,j}=\sum_{c',u,v} K^{(c)}_{c',u,v}\,h^{(c')}_{i+u,j+v}+b^{(c)}.
$$

Then $h_{\mathrm{new}}=\sigma(z)$ pointwise (ReLU, etc.). Stride and padding control output resolution.

### 2. Pooling

**Pooling** summarizes a local block (e.g. $2\times 2$ max or average) into one value. Effects: smaller maps, some local translation tolerance, larger effective receptive field per later unit. It is another hard constraint / downsampling choice in $\mathcal{H}$, not a learned dense mix of all pixels.

### 3. CNN as regularized MLP

Flatten the image and write a giant MLP. A convolutional layer corresponds to:

- sparsity pattern: each output depends on a patch;
- equality constraints: weights repeat across patches.

So CNN $\subset$ MLP in function-class terms (for matching shapes), with far fewer free parameters. Soft penalties like weight decay can still be added; the CNN structure is the main regularizer for vision.

### 4. Typical stack and classifier head

$$
\text{conv}\to\sigma\to\text{(pool)}\to\cdots\to\text{flatten / global pool}\to\text{dense / softmax}.
$$

Early layers: local patterns. Deeper layers: combinations over larger regions. Final dense layers map high-level features to labels. Train end-to-end by backprop on cross-entropy (or task loss).

### 5. Bridge

CNNs exploit **spatial** grid structure. Sequences (speech, text, time series) have **temporal** dependence with variable length — motivating recurrent nets next.

---

## Worked mini-example

CIFAR-style $32\times 32\times 3$ input. Layer 1: $16$ filters of size $3\times 3\times 3$ $\to$ about $16\times 27+16$ parameters, producing $16$ maps. Max-pool $2\times 2$ halves height/width. Another conv block, then flatten and a small dense classifier. A dense-only net on $32\times 32\times 3=3072$ inputs with comparable hidden width would need orders of magnitude more weights and ignore locality.

---

## Common confusions

| Confusion | Clarification |
|-----------|---------------|
| CNN $\neq$ neural net | CNN **is** a neural net with constrained connectivity / weights. |
| Pooling is required for UAT | UAT is about MLPs; pooling is a practical inductive bias, not universality. |
| Filters are hand-designed | Modern CNNs **learn** $K$ by ERM/backprop (classical SIFT-like features were hand-made). |
| Regularization only means $\lambda\|\theta\|^2$ | Architecture constraints are regularization too. |

2. In what sense is a CNN a “regularized MLP”?
3. What does max-pooling do to a $2\times 2$ block?
4. Why backprop still applies to CNNs?
5. Name one limitation of CNNs that RNNs address better.
